text:
jordan: Quick follow-up from the continuous-batcher RFC — we pulled a few metrics and I want to sync on two things: (1) where to draw the queue/ownership boundary between admission and the coalescer, and (2) how hard we should make preemption vs. soft-eviction. TL;DR: leaning to smaller surface = clearer invariants but more copying.

anika: +1 for the sync. can you paste the perf numbers you saw?

jordan: baseline:  p50 token latency for small requests (~8 tokens) jumped from 12ms -> 28ms when tenant A saturated GPU, but p95 only moved ~8ms. throughput stayed stable. suspicion: admission is admitting full request sets that blow out coalesce windows.

kevin: that matches an experiment i ran with micro-window sizing. when admission hands over opaque batches to coalescer we lose ability to *trim* based on headroom. two options: keep admission 'honest' (estimate headroom and cap) or let coalescer slice.

samira: Clarify terms: "admission" = decision to place task in queue pool; "coalescer" = the component that merges inflight requests into batches and schedules dispatch?

jordan: yes. admission decides if request enters lane X and reserves credit. coalescer groups and issues kernel work. we currently have admission reserve == requested tokens. coalescer could shrink actual kernel token count (via truncation/prefix cache) but that creates mismatch.

anika: Mismatch is the crux. If admission reserves full KV cache token, but coalescer truncates, we get phantom headroom and fairness harms.

kevin: proposals: 
- Option A: Tight contract. Admission must predict max kernel tokens and reserve that. Coalescer cannot change token footprint except via explicit eviction API. pros: accounting correct, simple fairness. cons: admissions must do heavier instrumentation / estimators.
- Option B: Loose contract. Admission reserves a hint; coalescer can shrink/expand at dispatch time and emits delta events that update ledger. pros: simpler admission, coalescer optimized for packing. cons: requires robust reconciliation and more churn under load.

samira: we tried Option B in the 2-week trial — delta events created spikes in ledger updates and our slot allocator had contention. ops-bot: noted 24% increase in control-plane ops during the test.

jordan: Right. Also thinking about preemption: earlier RFC favored soft-eviction (watermark-based) so we avoid killing in-progress KV. But under long tails that means low-priority tenants can starve.

anika: Could we do hybrid: soft-eviction normally, hard-preempt only when queue depth > hard-cutoff? e.g., soft up to 90% headroom, hard if > 120% of target.

kevin: That works but adds more modes. Implementation complexity: fastpath vs slowpath in admission. Fastpath can't stall on global signals. 

jordan: I sketched an interface: admission.reserve(tenant, tokens_hint) -> Reservation{lease_token, reserved_tokens, deadline_hint}. Coalescer.dispatch(lease_token, actual_tokens) -> dispatch_result{delta}. If delta < 0 we call ledger.adjust(tenant, delta). Simple.

samira: share code snippet for the proto?

jordan: ```proto
// fast sketch
message Reservation { string lease_token = 1; int32 reserved_tokens = 2; int64 expire_at = 3; }
rpc Reserve(ReserveRequest) returns (Reservation);
rpc Dispatch(DispatchRequest) returns (DispatchResult);
message DispatchResult { string lease_token = 1; int32 actual_tokens = 2; int32 delta = 3; }
```

anika: Two comments: (1) we need idempotency if coalescer retries dispatch after transient failure, (2) ledger.delta must be cheap (amortize per-batch).

kevin: On (1) capture attempt_id in Dispatch and ensure ops are idempotent. On (2) we bump per-tenant cohort counters, flush to main ledger on interval; that reduces hot updates but increases tail variance.

samira: Observability: want per-reservation tracing: reserved vs actual, truncation reason, eviction tags. Without that it's impossible to debug why tenant X got starved.

jordan: agreed. Also need a fallback policy: when coalescer decides to shrink a batch, we should prefer trimming tokens from best-effort tenants first (we already have priority classes). That reduces churn on critical tenants.

anika: Another trade: copying. If admission must be exact it needs to inspect the request payload (prompt length, growth delta), which may require copying payload metadata across processes. That adds memcopy cost and complexity. But not impossible — we already pass small headers.

kevin: From the runtime POV, copying metadata is cheap relative to kernel launch. The bigger cost is if admission blocks on KV cache lookup to estimate prefix hits. Blocking kills admission throughput. So any estimator must be async hint-based.

jordan: So practical path I propose: adopt Option A for critical tenants (enterprise SKUs) and Option B for best-effort. That keeps invariants for customers that need SLAs and lets us optimize packing for low-cost tiers.

samira: +1. Also we should add a "grace quota" for function-calling flows that often expand tokens mid-run. If not, we lose in-flight calls.

anika: Implementation plan? I can own admission changes, kevin owns coalescer delta, jordan will wire proto + telemetry.

jordan: timeline suggestion: 
- Week 1: land proto + minimal ledger.delta hook (no persistence)
- Week 2: instrument metrics and a canary on non-critical cluster
- Week 3: evaluate and flip critical-tenants to strict-mode

kevin: test matrix: synthetic microbursts, mixed tenant ratios (5:1:1), function-calls with mid-exec expansion. I'll add e2e harness.

samira: ops-bot: scheduled canary for Fri 09:00 UTC, cluster: staging-batcher-2.

anika: one last note: add a feature flag to switch delta reconciliation off if ledger pressure detected. don't want cascading control-plane spikes.

jordan: Good. I'll open the follow-up PR with proto + design doc. Thanks everyone. :thumbsup:

kevin: Thanks — excited to see if hybrid billing/fairness works in practice.

samira: thanks, closing the loop. ops-bot: canary created (#canary-834).
